gap: No result ChatGPT got puts a number on what the QNAP TVS-h674 costs once it has dual 10GbE: $1,899.00 for the i3 plus $269.00 for a QXG-10G2T card is $2,168.00, or $2,618.00 for the i5. That is $1,068.01 more than the UGREEN DXP6800 Pro (about $1,100), which has dual 10GbE built in. No result gives a yearly running cost either: about $58–67 for the UGREEN with four drives idling, from Notebookcheck's measured watts.
standout_why: I read four pages. Starry Hope (2026-11-02) quotes Notebookcheck's 37–42 W idle for the DXP6800 Pro but gives no kWh or dollars per year and nothing on QNAP card costs. Raidsize's best 6-bay page doesn't cover the TVS-h674, and it has no card price, no total cost and no wattage. The QNAP spec page that ChatGPT cited says 10GbE is 'Optional via PCIe expansion card' and lists the card models but no prices. Notebookcheck has the watts but doesn't turn them into a yearly cost. The ChatGPT answers call the QNAP 'considerably more expensive once you add 10GbE' but never give the figure. None of these pages states the card price or a 10GbE-ready total.
decides: It backs up ChatGPT's pick, the UGREEN DXP6800 Pro, with numbers. Getting dual 10GbE on the cheapest QNAP TVS-h674 costs about twice as much ($2,168.00 against $1,099.99). Its 6-drive standby figure from QNAP (39.9 W, about $63 a year) isn't lower than the UGREEN's measured 4-drive idle range. So for a Plex and 10GbE buyer the QNAP's extra cost buys ZFS and VMs, not lower running costs. The TerraMaster F6-425 Pro could still undercut the UGREEN, but I couldn't open a price for it today.

findings.label: Price to dual 10GbE (derived)

findings.label: Price (Notebookcheck's price box)

findings.source_title: Great hardware, not quite there yet - Ugreen NASync DXP6800 Pro review - Notebookcheck
findings.note: UGREEN's US store returned HTTP 429 three times, so this price comes from Notebookcheck's page. ChatGPT's cards showed the same $1,099.99 at Newegg and Best Buy. Dual 10GbE is built in, so there is no card to add: price to dual 10GbE = $1,099.99.

findings.label: Measured idle power (Notebookcheck, Daniel Schmidt)
findings.value: 36.59–41.93 W idle with 4× Seagate IronWolf 4 TB; 22.40 W idle with no drives
findings.source_title: Great hardware, not quite there yet - Ugreen NASync DXP6800 Pro review - Notebookcheck
findings.note: Published 2026-07-01, updated 2026-10-05. The same review measured 9.5 Gbit/s with iPerf3 on 10GbE, sending and receiving. It ran no Plex transcode test.

findings.label: Yearly idle running cost, 4 drives (derived)
findings.source_title: Notebookcheck DXP6800 Pro review + EIA Electric Power Monthly Table 5.6.A
findings.note: 36.59 W × 8,760 h = 320.5 kWh × $0.1816 = $58.21; 41.93 W × 8,760 h = 367.3 kWh × $0.1816 = $66.70. The rate is the EIA US average residential price for Aug 2026 (preliminary), from https://www.eia.gov/electricity/monthly/epm_table_grapher.php?t=epmt_5_6_a. Assumes 24/7 idle.

findings.label: Maker-rated power, 6 drives fitted
findings.value: 39.911 W with disks in standby; 79.363 W typical operating (all bays filled with WD10EFRX)
findings.note: The same figures are given for the i3 and the i5. These are QNAP's own numbers, not a reviewer's measurement, and they leave out the power the 10GbE card draws.

findings.label: Yearly running cost (derived)
findings.value: Disk standby 349.6 kWh/yr ≈ $63.49/yr; typical operating 695.2 kWh/yr ≈ $126.25/yr
findings.source_title: TVS-h674 | Hardware Specs | QNAP (US) + EIA Table 5.6.A
findings.note: 39.911 W × 8,760 h = 349.6 kWh × $0.1816 = $63.49; 79.363 W × 8,760 h = 695.2 kWh × $0.1816 = $126.25. Not directly comparable with the UGREEN figure: these are QNAP's numbers with 6 drives spun down, against Notebookcheck's measurement with 4 drives spinning idle.
